---
title: "Under-sampling"
description: "A data-balancing approach that reduces the number of examples from a majority class."
term: "Under-sampling"
letter: "U"
category: "Data Engineering"
difficulty: "Intermediate"
---

## Simple explanation

Under-sampling reduces the number of examples from a common class so a
training set is less dominated by that class. It can make training more
balanced, but discarded examples may contain useful variation.

## Technical explanation

Under-sampling selects a subset of majority-class observations, either
randomly or using a rule such as near-miss selection. It changes the
training class distribution and may alter the learned decision boundary;
probability estimates and threshold behavior may need recalibration to
match deployment prevalence.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Class imbalance can make a learner favor the majority class. Under-sampling
can reduce training cost and increase minority influence, but it risks
information loss and can create a mismatch between training and production
distributions.

## How it works

Apply the sampling strategy only to the training data, leaving validation
and test sets representative of the intended population. Train the model,
then evaluate relevant class-specific metrics and calibration on
untouched, representative data.

## Practical example

A fraud classifier might retain a subset of legitimate transactions while
keeping all observed fraud examples during training. Evaluate it at the
realistic production class prevalence and tune alert thresholds using
appropriate validation data.

## Common misconceptions

- Balancing the training set does not automatically make a model fair or
  improve minority-class performance.
- Resampling before a train-test split can leak information and make
  evaluation overly optimistic.
